title: Air pushes: why a card holds up a glass of water, and nothing really sucks

summary.text: Fill a glass to the brim, slide a card over it, and turn it upside down. The card stays put and the water stays in. Nothing is gluing the card on. The air is pushing it, with about one kilogram of push on every square centimetre. You will test a bottle that stops pouring when you screw the cap on, a straw that stops working when it has a hole, and a bottle that squashes itself. You find out why we never notice the push of air, why sucking is really air pushing, why a straw or a pump can lift water only about ten metres, and why your ears pop on a hill.
summary.art: A full glass turned upside down over a basin with a playing card holding in the water, and small arrows pushing up on the card from the air below.

intro.hook: Fill a glass to the brim and slide a card over it. Hold the card and turn the glass upside down. Now take your hand away. The card does not fall. The water does not fall. What is holding it up?
intro.text: There is no glue, no magnet and no hand. Something you cannot see is pushing the card up from below, and it is strong enough to hold a glass of water. In this unit you find out what it is. You test a bottle with a hole, a straw with a hole and a bottle that crushes itself. You also find out how people first proved that air has a push, and why it lifts water only ten metres and no more.
intro.art: A child holding a glass of water upside down over a basin, with a card staying in place at the rim and no hand under it.

outcomes: I can explain that air pushes on everything it touches, from every direction, with about 1 kilogram of push on each square centimetre.
I can explain why we do not notice the push of air, even though it is very strong.
I can explain why a card holds the water in an upside-down glass, and why water stops running out of a capped bottle with a hole.
I can explain that suction is not a pull from an empty place, but a push from the side that has more air.
I can say what happens to air pressure as you go up a hill or a mountain, and why your ears pop.
I can run a fair test with a control, and say my claim, my evidence and my reasoning.
I can use area and weight to work out how big a push of air is on a surface.
I can explain how Torricelli's tube showed that air has weight, and why a straw or a pump can lift water only about ten metres.

terms.meaning: The deep layer of air that wraps around the whole Earth. Gravity holds it there.
terms.example: We live at the bottom of the atmosphere, which is like a deep sea of air.
terms.art: The Earth seen from space with a thin blue layer of air around it.

terms.meaning: How hard something pushes on each square centimetre of a surface.
terms.example: A drawing pin has a point so small that all your push is squeezed onto a tiny spot, and the pressure is very high.
terms.art: A thumb pressing a drawing pin into a board, with the point tiny and the flat end wide.

terms.meaning: The push of air on every surface it touches. It comes from billions of air particles hitting the surface every second.
terms.example: Air pressure at sea level pushes with about 1 kilogram of weight on every square centimetre.
terms.art: A flat hand with small arrows pressing on it from all sides, and tiny particles bouncing on the skin.

terms.meaning: How much flat surface something has, counted in square centimetres.
terms.example: A card 10 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide has an area of 60 square centimetres.
terms.art: A card on squared paper with the squares counted along its length and width.

terms.meaning: Two pushes that are equal and opposite, so a thing does not move.
terms.example: When you press your palms together as hard as you can, neither hand moves.
terms.art: Two palms pressed together with equal arrows pointing at each other.

terms.meaning: A space with no air in it, or almost none.
terms.example: Space between the planets is nearly a vacuum.
terms.art: A glass jar with the air pumped out and a few tiny particles floating inside.

terms.meaning: The word for what happens when some air is taken away from one side of a thing, so the air on the other side pushes the thing towards the gap.
terms.example: When you sip through a straw, air pushing on your drink in the glass lifts the drink up the straw.
terms.art: A straw in a glass with arrows pushing down on the drink in the glass and nothing pushing on the drink in the straw.

terms.meaning: An instrument that measures air pressure.
terms.example: A barometer on a weather station falls when a storm is coming.
terms.art: A round dial barometer on a wall with a pointer between the words rain and fair.

terms.meaning: How high a place is above the sea.
terms.example: Ooty is at an altitude of about 2,200 metres, so its air pushes less than the air in Chennai.
terms.art: A hill with a flag at the top marked 2,200 metres and a beach at the bottom marked 0.

terms.meaning: A hand pump with its working part down in the water, so it pushes the water up the pipe instead of waiting for the air to push it up.
terms.example: The India Mark II hand pump has its cylinder deep down inside the borehole.
terms.art: A village hand pump with a cut-away pipe showing the cylinder far below the ground in the water.

terms.meaning: A silvery metal that is liquid at room temperature and about 13.6 times heavier than the same amount of water. It is poisonous, so never play with it.
terms.example: Torricelli used mercury in his tube because mercury is so heavy that a short tube of it balances the push of the air.
terms.art: A glass tube with a shiny silver liquid, with a skull-and-crossbones warning label beside it.

terms.meaning: To spread out into more space.
terms.example: A sealed packet of chips puffs up when you take it up a hill, because the air inside expands.
terms.art: A small flat packet of chips at the bottom of a hill and a puffed-up packet at the top.

terms.meaning: A tiny piece of matter, much too small to see. Air is made of particles that fly about in every direction.
terms.example: One breath holds far more air particles than there are grains of sand on every beach on Earth, going by the usual estimate.
terms.art: Many small coloured balls flying in all directions inside a box, with arrows showing them hitting the walls.

terms.meaning: A tube that moves liquid up and over a rim and down to a lower place, with no pouring or pumping once it starts.
terms.example: A farmer can empty a tank into a lower field through a pipe full of water.
terms.art: A water tank on a high stand with a bent pipe over the rim leading to a bucket on the ground.

explanations.concept: Air pushes on everything it touches, from every direction
explanations.definition: Air pressure is the push of air on a surface. The air pushes on the top, the bottom and the sides of every thing in it, all at once.
explanations.description: Air is made of particles that fly about and bump into whatever they meet. Each bump is a tiny push. A surface is hit billions of times every second, so the tiny pushes add up to one steady push. Because the particles fly in every direction, the push is the same in every direction. It pushes down on the top of the table. It pushes up on the underside. It pushes sideways on the wall. This is why the card on the glass holds when the glass is turned sideways too.
examples: Air pushes on your whole body all day, on your front, your back and your sides.
A card held under an upside-down glass is pushed up by the air below it.
A closed bottle taken to a hill station swells or squashes because the air outside pushes differently there.
explanations.art: A flat card in the air with arrows pushing on it from above, below and both sides, all the same length.

explanations.concept: How big the push is: about 1 kilogram on each square centimetre
explanations.definition: At sea level, air presses on each square centimetre with about 1 kilogram of weight. On a table 1 metre by 1 metre, that is about 10 tonnes.
explanations.description: The air above you is a tall pile, going up about a hundred kilometres before it thins away. That air has weight, and the weight of the pile above a patch of ground pushes down on it. The pile above one square centimetre weighs about 1 kilogram. A child's flat hand is about 70 square centimetres. So the air pushes on each side of the hand with a weight of about 70 kilograms. Air pushes sideways and up just as hard as it pushes down, because its particles bump into things from every direction.
examples: On a patch as big as your thumbnail, the air pushes with about the weight of a packet of sugar.
A door 2 metres high and 1 metre wide has about 20 tonnes of air pushing on each side of it.
The push on a postcard is about 150 kilograms on each side.
explanations.art: A child's flat hand with a label that says 70 square centimetres, and a big sack of rice beside it marked 70 kilograms.

explanations.concept: Why we do not notice the push
explanations.definition: We do not notice air pressure because it is balanced. The air pushes in from outside, and the fluids and air inside our bodies push out with the same strength.
explanations.description: A push that is balanced does not move anything, so we do not notice it. Inside your body there is air in your lungs, and your blood, your cells and your gut are full of water. They all push outward at the same strength as the air outside pushes inward. We feel the push only when it changes quickly, as in an aeroplane or a lift going up a tall building, because then the outside push changes and the inside one takes a little while to catch up. That is the pop in your ears.
examples: You do not notice the push of about 70 kilograms of air on each side of your hand.
Your ears pop in a fast lift because the push outside has changed.
A fish in the deep sea does not notice the huge push of water on her, because her body pushes back.
explanations.art: A child standing with arrows pointing inwards on the skin and arrows of the same size pointing outwards from inside the body.

explanations.concept: Why a card holds the water in an upside-down glass
explanations.definition: The card stays on because the air pushes up on it much harder than the water pushes down on it.
explanations.description: A glass of water 10 centimetres tall pushes down on the card with about 10 grams of weight on each square centimetre. The air below pushes up with about 1,000 grams on each square centimetre. The air wins by about 100 times. For the water to fall, the card has to move away, and the water has to leave a gap above it. If the glass is full to the brim, there is no air in the glass to fill the gap, so the water cannot fall. The only way the water can go is if the card bends a little and lets some air in. A smooth, flat card stops that.
examples: A card held over a full tumbler turned upside down.
A full bottle with a hole low down stops dripping when the cap is on.
A drinks tin with one hole in the top pours slowly and in jerks, and with two holes it pours smoothly.
explanations.art: A glass upside down with a card, an upward arrow of air as long as a ruler and a tiny downward arrow of water.

explanations.concept: Nothing sucks: suction is a push from the side that has more air
explanations.definition: A straw does not pull a drink. It takes some air out of the straw, so less air pushes on the drink inside it. The air pushing on the drink in the glass then lifts the drink up the straw.
explanations.description: When you sip, you make the space inside your mouth bigger, and the air in your mouth and straw spreads out and pushes less. The air outside is now pushing harder on the drink in the glass than the air in the straw is pushing on the drink inside the straw. The harder push wins, and the drink goes up. A hole in the straw lets air in, so the push inside the straw is as big as the push outside again, and the drink stays down. A vacuum cleaner, a suction hook and a dropper all work this way.
examples: A straw with a hole in it does not work. Cover the hole with a finger and it works again.
A suction hook stays on a tile because the air outside pushes it flat against the tile.
A dropper fills when you squeeze it, put it in water, and let go.
explanations.art: A straw in a glass of juice with a big arrow pushing down on the juice in the glass, and nothing pushing on the juice inside the straw.

explanations.concept: Air pressure falls as you go up
explanations.definition: The higher you go, the less air is above you, so the air pushes less. At the top of Mount Everest, the push is about one third of the push at sea level.
explanations.description: Air is heaviest at the bottom, because it is squashed by all the air above it. As you climb, there is less air above you, and the air around you is thinner. At 5,500 metres, which is about as high as a base camp on Everest, the push is about half the push at sea level. A sealed bottle taken up a mountain swells, because the air inside still pushes at sea-level strength and the air outside pushes less. Taken down again, it squashes. Weather also changes air pressure a little each day, and a falling reading often means a storm is on its way.
examples: A packet of chips puffs up on the way to Ooty or Munnar.
Aeroplane cabins are kept at the push you would feel at about 2,000 metres, not the push at the height the plane flies.
Cooking takes longer high in the hills, because water boils at a lower temperature there.
explanations.art: A mountain with three labels, sea level, halfway up and the top, and air particles getting fewer on the way up.

explanations.concept: How far air can lift water: about ten metres
explanations.definition: The push of the air can hold up a column of water about 10 metres tall. This is why a straw or a pump at the top of a pipe cannot lift water from deeper than about 10 metres.
explanations.description: Think of a tube standing in a tank of water, with all the air taken out of the tube. The air pushes on the water in the tank and forces water up the tube. The water stops rising when the weight of the water in the tube equals the push of the air. At sea level that happens at about 10.3 metres. Torricelli used mercury, which is 13.6 times heavier than water, so the column was 13.6 times shorter, about 76 centimetres. In real pumps the limit is a bit lower, about 7 or 8 metres, because some air always leaks in. For deeper wells, the pump is put down in the water and pushes the water up.
examples: A mercury barometer stands at about 76 centimetres.
A hand pump on top of a borewell stops working when the water falls below about 7 metres.
An India Mark II pump has its cylinder deep down so it can work from much deeper.
explanations.art: Two tubes side by side, one with water 10 metres high and one with silver mercury 76 centimetres high, both standing in open dishes.

explanations.concept: Pressure at the level of particles
explanations.definition: Pressure is made by particles hitting a surface. More particles in the same space, or faster particles, mean more hits and a bigger push.
explanations.description: Take a bicycle pump and press the plunger with your finger over the hole. The same air is squeezed into less space. The particles are closer and hit the walls more often, so the push grows. Warm the air and the particles move faster, so each bump is harder, and the push grows again. A sealed bottle of hot air that cools has fewer and slower bumps, and the pressure inside falls. This is what happens in the Bottle That Squashes Itself. The particles are tiny and always moving, so even still air is a very busy place.
examples: A pumped-up tyre has more particles in the same space, so it pushes hard.
A hot sealed bottle that is cooled pushes less on its walls.
A pressure cooker raises the push inside, so water boils at a higher temperature.
explanations.art: Two boxes of flying particles, one with a few and one with many, with longer arrows on the walls of the box with many.

explanations.description: A siphon is a tube full of water that carries water up over a rim and down to a lower place. Everyone agrees on what a siphon does. Scientists still argue about the best way to explain why it works. The old textbook explanation says the push of the air on the water in the top tank is what drives the water up and over. Some experiments suggest that this is not the whole story.
examples: A farmer empties a tank into a lower field through a pipe.
A fish tank cleaner moves dirty water into a bucket through a tube.
Some experiments have kept a siphon running with much of the air pressure taken away.
explanations.art: A tube arching over the rim of a high tank into a bucket below, with arrows showing water flowing down the long side.

perspectives.who: The air pressure explanation, found in many older textbooks
perspectives.explanation: The air pushes on the water in the top tank and forces it up and over the bend. The siphon would stop in a place with no air.

perspectives.who: The chain explanation, supported by some physicists who tested siphons at low pressure
perspectives.explanation: The water in the tube acts like a chain, because its particles stick to each other. The longer, heavier side of the chain falls down and pulls the rest after it. Some experiments report siphons running at much lower pressure, which suggests that air pressure is not what drives them. Others, such as Richert and Binder in 2011, tested this and found that pressure still matters.

agreed.text: Air has weight and pushes on everything it touches, from every direction.
agreed.evidence: Torricelli's mercury tube, tried around 1643, and thousands of barometers since then show that the air's push holds up a column of mercury about 76 centimetres tall.

agreed.text: At sea level, air pushes with about 1 kilogram of weight on each square centimetre.
agreed.evidence: This has been measured with barometers in every country. The reading is about 1,013 millibars at sea level on an average day.

agreed.text: Air pressure falls as you go higher, and the atmosphere has no sharp top.
agreed.evidence: Périer's climb of the Puy de Dôme in 1648 showed this, and so have many balloon, aeroplane and mountain readings since.

agreed.text: Drinking through a straw, using a suction hook and running a vacuum cleaner all work because air pushes from the side that has more of it.
agreed.evidence: The straw stops working when a hole lets the air in, and starts again when the hole is covered.

agreed.text: The push on a thing is the pressure multiplied by its area.
agreed.evidence: In the same air, a large flat surface such as a door gets a much bigger total push than a small one such as a card.

challenging.claim: Nature hates empty space, so water has to follow a pump's piston to fill the gap.
challenging.who: Aristotle and many thinkers for nearly 2,000 years.
challenging.for: Water does follow a piston up a pipe, and a gap never seemed to open.
challenging.against: Pumps stop working above about 10 metres, so the 'hatred' has a limit. Torricelli's tube made a real empty space at the top, and nature did not fill it.

challenging.claim: Suction pulls things towards an empty place.
challenging.who: Many people, and most everyday speech.
challenging.for: It feels like the straw pulls the drink, and the word is used everywhere.
challenging.against: A hole in the straw stops the drink rising, even though you sip just as hard. An empty space has nothing in it to pull with. The push comes from the air on the other side.

challenging.claim: Air pressure pushes down, because the air is above us.
challenging.for: The weight of the air above does cause the pressure.
challenging.against: In the Card on the Glass, the card held the water even when the glass was tilted onto its side. Air pushes sideways and up just as hard, because its particles fly in every direction.

challenging.claim: A tall tree lifts water like a straw, using the push of the air.
challenging.who: Many people, because it is a natural guess.
challenging.for: Water goes up a tree just as water goes up a straw.
challenging.against: The push of air can lift water only about 10 metres, but some trees are over 100 metres tall. Scientists think the leaves pull the water up. The water holds together like a chain, because its particles stick to each other. The details are still debated.

challenging.claim: A fall in air pressure usually means that rain or a storm is on the way.
challenging.who: Weather forecasters and sailors for over 300 years.
challenging.for: In many places, low pressure goes with clouds, rain and wind.
challenging.against: Pressure alone does not tell you the weather. A forecast also needs temperature, wind and water in the air.

big_questions.q: About 70 kilograms of air pushes on each side of your hand, and you feel nothing. If a push is the same on every side, is it still a push?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when you take the air from one side away.

big_questions.q: A deep-sea fish lives with a push on her body a hundred times bigger than the push we feel. For her, is that push big, small, or just normal?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is doing the feeling.

big_questions.q: Is a vacuum cleaner sucking or is the air pushing? Does it matter which word we use?
big_questions.hint: In the Straw with a Hole, the hole stopped the drink rising. Think about why, and about what the word 'suck' makes us picture.

big_questions.q: Space is almost a vacuum. A rocket going up leaves the air behind. How does an astronaut stay alive, and what does she carry along with her?
big_questions.hint: Think about the push of the air on a body, and the air inside it.

big_questions.q: For 2,000 years people trusted Aristotle's famous idea that nature hates an empty space. Then Torricelli tested it. How do you decide when to trust an old idea, and when to test it?
big_questions.hint: Well-makers in Italy saw that their pumps would not lift water higher than about ten metres. Think about who listened to them.

big_questions.q: Air pushes from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side, and that makes wind. Does a big wind start from a small difference in pushes?
big_questions.hint: Think about the straw. What does a small difference in push do to a drink?

big_questions.q: The air is part of you every time you breathe. Where does the air end and you begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air in your lungs a second ago, and a second from now.

story.title: The Pump That Ran Out of Push
story.note: A made-up story. The village, the people and the pump repair are imagined. The science in it is real. A pump at the top of a pipe can lift water only about ten metres at most, and for deeper water the working part of the pump is put down in the water, as in the India Mark II hand pump.
text: In the last week of May, the hand pump beside the temple tank in Marungulam began to cough. Marungulam was a village near Thanjavur, and Selvi, who was nine, had pumped that handle every morning since she was six. Clang, clang, clang. Air hissed from the spout. Then one thin dribble came, and then nothing at all.

By evening half the village stood around the pump. Murugesan, the ward member, kicked the iron base. 'The pump is old,' he said. 'It has lost its pull. We need a stronger one.' Kumar, who drove the tractor, nodded. 'Bring the biggest pump from town,' he said. 'It will pull water up from anywhere.'

Next morning the block office sent Revathi, a hand pump mechanic with a canvas bag of spanners. She said very little. She opened the head of the pump, looked at the leather washer, and closed it again. 'The washer is fine,' she said. 'The pump is fine.'

'Then why is there no water?' asked Murugesan. Revathi tied a steel nut to a ball of string with a knot every metre. 'Selvi, hold the end and count the knots as I let it down the pipe.' The string ran into the dark. Selvi counted aloud. 'Eight. Nine. Ten. Eleven.' The nut stopped with a tiny plop. 'Twelve,' said Selvi, 'nearly twelve.' Only the last knot came up wet.
'The water has gone down twelve metres,' said Revathi. 'The rains were poor, and every house in the village has been taking water from the ground.'

'Then we need a stronger pull,' said Kumar again. Revathi smiled. She took a bottle of lime juice and a straw out of her bag. 'Kumar Anna, sip this.' Kumar sipped. 'Good,' he said. With a pin, Revathi made a hole in the straw, near the top. 'Sip again.' Kumar sipped and sipped, until his face was red. The juice stayed where it was. Somebody laughed.

'You pulled just as hard,' said Revathi. 'Nothing came.' She put her thumb over the hole. The juice rose at once. 'A straw does not pull the juice. A pump does not pull water. They only take the air out of the pipe above the water. Then the air outside pushes on the water in the bottle, and that push drives it up the pipe. The hole let air back in, so there was no difference in pushes.'

'Air pushing?' said Murugesan. 'Air is nothing.' 'On a patch as big as your thumbnail, it pushes with the weight of a packet of sugar,' said Revathi. 'On the whole top of a well, it is thousands of tonnes. But that push can hold up only about ten metres of water. Your water is at twelve. A bigger pump at the top would make no difference. Nothing could push water that high from there.'
Nobody spoke. A crow shouted from the tamarind tree. 'So what do we do?' asked Murugesan at last, quite softly.

'We stop asking the top of the pipe to do the lifting,' said Revathi. 'We put the working part of the pump down in the water. Then it pushes the water up the pipe from below, a bit at a time, and it does not have to wait for the air to lift the water.'

It took two days. Murugesan, Kumar and six others pulled the heavy pipes out one by one, each as long as a man is tall. Revathi sat on a stool and gave orders. Selvi chalked a number on every pipe so that they would go back in the right order. At the end, the new part went down on long rods: a cylinder with a piston and a leather cup, which sat deep in the wet dark, twelve metres below the road.

On the second evening Revathi said, 'Selvi, you try.' Clang. Clang. A cough. Then water came, cold and clear, in a fat rope, into a steel pot. The whole street cheered. Murugesan filled a tumbler first and gave it to Revathi.

That night, at home, Selvi found a straw in the kitchen and poked it with her mother's pin. She poured a glass of buttermilk and sipped. Nothing. She put her thumb over the hole. Up came the buttermilk, cold and sour. She looked at the straw. 'Nobody pulled you,' she told the buttermilk. 'The whole sky pushed you.'
story.epiphany: A straw or a pump does not pull water. It takes the air away from one side, and the air on the other side pushes the water up. That push is strong, but it can lift water only about ten metres.
ask: Why can a pump at the top of a pipe never lift water from deeper than about ten metres, however strong the pump is?
Why did the juice stop rising when there was a hole in the straw, even though Kumar sipped just as hard?
If you could take a straw to the Moon, where there is no air, could you drink a drink with it? Why?

roots.context: We have found that air pushes on everything, that you never notice it, and that sucking is really air pushing. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Nothing sucks. When you sip through a straw, you take air out of the straw, so less air pushes on the drink inside it. The air pushing on the drink in the glass lifts it up. Suction is always a push from the side that has more air.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'suck' and picture the empty place pulling. But an empty place has nothing in it to pull with. The word makes us look at the gap, when the push comes from the other side.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Straw with a Hole, the straw with a hole near the top did not work, though the sip was just as hard. Covering the hole made it work again. Torricelli's tube stopped at 76 centimetres because the air's push, not a pull from the empty space, held the mercury up.

three.who_am_i: About 70 kilograms of air pushes on each side of your hand, and you feel nothing. You are held in shape by pushes that balance.
three.what_is_life: A fish, a bird and a tree each live in a place where the air or water pushes with a different strength, and each body pushes back from inside. A body fits the pressure it grew up in.
three.what_is_this_world: We live at the bottom of a deep sea of air. Wind, weather, a straw and a pump all happen because the push is bigger in one place than in another.

roots.thread: Still air looks empty and calm. Zoom in and it is billions of particles, flying and hitting every surface every second. The calm is a balance of countless tiny pushes. A straw, a pump, the wind and a storm all begin when one push is a little bigger than another. Where we see nothing, there is a great deal going on, held in balance.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 10.168, the hymn to Vata, the wind
teachings.teaching: Hymn 10.168 of the Rig Veda says that the sound of the wind is heard but its form is not seen, and it calls the wind the self, or breath, of the gods (verse 4, as paraphrased).
teachings.link: We cannot see air, but we know it by what it does. It holds a card on a glass of water and lifts a drink up a straw.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, fragment B51 (Diels and Kranz numbering), ancient Greece, about 500 BCE
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus said that things hold together by pulling against each other in opposite directions, like the string and the wood of a bow or a lyre.
teachings.link: The card holds because the water pushes down and the air pushes up. The balance of two opposite pushes keeps it still.

science.text: Pressure comes from air particles hitting a surface billions of times every second. Their number and their speed set the size of the push.
Empty space is never quite empty. Experiments have measured a tiny push between two metal plates in a vacuum, the Casimir effect.

other_view.view: A difference in pressure can be described either way. 'The air pushes the drink up' and 'the straw sucks the drink up' are two ways of describing the same difference. The sums come out the same. So the word suction is fine for daily life, as long as we remember that nothing pulls from an empty place.

practice.title: Two pushes that cancel
practice.say: Sit still and put your palms together in front of your chest. Push gently, then harder, then harder still. Notice that neither hand moves. Two strong pushes can look like nothing at all. Now relax your hands. Breathe in slowly three times. Feel the air coming in and going out. The air outside and the air in your chest are pushing on each other all day, in perfect balance.
practice.kid: Press your palms together. Push hard. Neither hand moves. Two strong pushes can look like nothing. Now breathe in slowly three times. Feel the air go in and out.

ask: If a push is the same on every side, and you feel nothing, what else around you might be pushing without you noticing?
A fish in the deep sea lives with a push on her body a hundred times bigger than the push we feel. Is that push big, or small, or just normal? Who decides?
Is a vacuum cleaner sucking, or is the air pushing? Does it matter which word we use?
The air in your lungs a second ago is now in the room. Where does the air end and you begin?

games.title: Who Pushes Harder? A card game about air
games.context: This game uses cards about things that squash, swell, stick and lift. For each card you decide which air pushes harder, the air outside or the air inside, or whether they push the same.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with three tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the others put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else puts one token face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up together, and the reader turning the card over to show the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a squashing, swelling or sticking puzzle on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A full glass is turned upside down with a card on it. What holds the card?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. The air below pushes up on the card with about 100 times more force than the water pushes down.

items.f: A thin bottle is filled with steam, closed, and then cooled. It crumples. Why?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. The steam turned back to water and the air inside cooled, so the inside pushed less.

items.f: A sealed packet of chips is taken up a hill to Ooty. It puffs up. Why?
items.b: Inside air pushes harder. The air outside is thinner up there, so it pushes less on the packet than the air inside does.

items.f: An open bottle sits on a table in a room. Which air pushes harder on its walls?
items.b: Both push the same. The bottle is open, so the air inside and the air outside are one air.

items.f: A rubber suction hook is pressed onto a smooth tile and holds a towel. What keeps it on?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. Little air is left under the cup, so the air outside pushes it flat.

items.f: You sip juice through a straw. What lifts the juice?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. The air on the juice in the glass pushes more than the thin air in the straw does.

items.f: You sip through a straw that has a big hole near the top. The juice does not rise. Why?
items.b: Both push the same. The hole lets air in, so the air in the straw pushes as hard as the air outside.

items.f: A cycle tyre is pumped up hard. Which air pushes harder on the rubber?
items.b: Inside air pushes harder. The pump squeezed more air particles into the same space, so they hit the rubber harder.

items.f: The weight on top of a pressure cooker begins to lift and the whistle sounds. Which push is bigger?
items.b: Inside air and steam push harder. The cooker traps the steam, so the push inside gets bigger than the push outside.

items.f: A jar of jam is sealed while hot. As it cools, the button on its lid goes down. Why?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. As the air in the jar cools, it pushes less, and the outside air pushes the lid in.

items.f: A closed, empty bottle is carried from Ooty down to Chennai. It gets a little squashed. Why?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. Chennai is at sea level, so the air there pushes more than the thin air that was shut in on the hill.

items.f: An aeroplane is coming down to land, and your ears feel pushed in. Which push is bigger?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. The air gets denser as the plane goes down, and the air in your ear has not caught up yet.

items.f: An aeroplane is climbing after take-off, and your ears feel full. Which push is bigger?
items.b: Inside air pushes harder. The air outside is getting thinner, and the air in your ear has not escaped yet.

items.f: You squeeze a rubber dropper, put it in water, and let go. Water goes in. Why?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. Letting go lowers the push inside the dropper, so the air on the water outside pushes the water in.

items.f: A vacuum cleaner is switched on and dust goes in from the floor. What pushes the dust in?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. The machine lowers the push inside, and the air in the room pushes the dust and air in.

items.f: A bottle of fizzy drink is still closed. Which push is bigger on the cap?
items.b: Inside gas pushes harder. The gas in the drink is squeezed to several times the push of the air outside, and the cap holds it in.

items.f: A deep-sea fish is pulled up fast to the surface. Her swim bladder swells. Why?
items.b: Inside gas pushes harder. The water pushed on her body very hard in the deep, and at the surface that push is gone, so the gas inside expands.

items.f: A boiled egg sits on the mouth of a bottle. The air inside the bottle is made to cool, and the egg is pushed in. Why?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. When the air inside cools, it pushes less, so the outside air pushes the egg in.

items.f: A closed plastic bottle of water is left in a hot car and its sides bulge. Why?
items.b: Inside air pushes harder. The hot air inside has faster particles that hit the walls harder.

items.f: A tied balloon is put in the fridge and it shrinks a little. Why?
items.b: Outside air pushes harder. The cold air inside has slower particles that push less, so the balloon gets smaller until the pushes match.

printables.title: 9 tokens: three that say Outside pushes harder, three that say Inside pushes harder, and three that say Both push the same

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first words on the back scores one point.
A player who also gives a correct reason, using the words push, particles, cools or thinner, scores one more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With one player, you are the reader and the guesser. Put your token down, then turn the card to check, and keep your own score.
With two players, swap the reader's job after every card.
The game ends when all 20 cards have been read. The highest score wins.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the 9 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one of each kind of token.
flow.say: These cards show things that squash, swell, stick and lift. For each card, we decide which air pushes harder. Is it the air outside, the air inside, or are they the same?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take one of each token.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Pushes Harder. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: Up to four can play: one reader and up to three guessers, because there are three of each token. One child plays alone with a parent as the reader.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card four, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone puts a token down. Turn them over together. Now read the back. Who scored? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the cards where the outside pushes harder have in common?
good: Something took away some of the air inside.
The air inside was cooled, thinned or let out.
The push inside was smaller than outside.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards and learn how the scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Keep score. Ask your child to say each reason before you read the back.
flow.say: Keep going. This time, say your reason before the reader turns the card over. Why did you pick that token?
flow.kid: Play eight more cards. Say your reason before you check.
flow.parent: If your child picks Both push the same for a card where something is moving, ask what is making the thing move. When nothing is moving, the pushes usually match.
flow.context: In this step, you play the next eight cards and give reasons before the answer is shown.

flow.do: Play the last four cards. Count the points. Ask your child which card surprised them most, and why.
flow.say: Last four cards. Then we count. Which card surprised you most? What did you think before you saw the back?
flow.kid: Play the last four cards. Count your points. Which one surprised you?
flow.think: Is there any card where nothing was pushing at all?
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game, count the points, and talk about the card that surprised you most.

experiments.title: The Bottle with a Hole: when does the water stop?
experiments.question: A bottle of water has a small hole near the bottom. With the cap off, the water runs out. What happens with the cap screwed on tight? What happens if there is a second hole high up?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. With the cap on tight, will the water keep running out of the hole, or stop? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same bottle, the same hole and the same amount of water are used in every test. Only one thing changes at a time: the cap on or off, or a second hole. You count the seconds the water flows in the same way each time, and stop counting at 30. The test with the cap off is the control. It shows what the hole does when nothing else is changed.

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle of 1 litre with its cap, with smooth sides
a sewing needle or the point of a compass, to make small holes about 1 millimetre wide (a grown-up uses this)
a folded towel to hold the bottle on while the holes are made
a small piece of sticky tape, to cover the hole while you fill the bottle
a big basin or a clean sink to catch the water
a phone or clock with a second hand
a marker pen
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes with the pointed tool, with the bottle on a folded towel, and pushes away from their hands. Do the test over a basin or a sink. Wipe up spilt water at once so nobody slips.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for each test. Then draw the bottle with the hole, and draw arrows for the air at the hole and at the top of the water. Say which air is pushing in which place.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a small hole in a water bottle. You find out when the water runs out, and when it stops, and what the air has to do with it.

setup.art: A clear 1-litre bottle lying on a folded towel with a grown-up pushing a needle through its side, about 4 centimetres from the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a small hole near the bottom.

setup.art: A bottle of water held over a basin with a finger on the hole and the cap screwed on tight.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the bottle, close the cap tight, and cover the hole with a finger.

setup.art: The same bottle over a basin with the finger lifted, a few drops falling and then stopping, and a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Lift your finger. Count the seconds the water keeps flowing.

setup.art: The same bottle with the cap unscrewed and a clear stream of water coming from the hole into the basin.
setup.caption: 4. Take the cap off. Count the seconds again.

setup.art: A bottle with a second small hole high on the side, above the water level, and a steady stream from the bottom hole.
setup.caption: 5. A grown-up makes a second hole high up. Cap on. What happens now?

flow.do: Show your child the bottle, the needle and the basin. Say that you will make a hole in the bottle. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will put a small hole near the bottom of this bottle and fill it with water. If I screw the cap on tight and take my finger off the hole, what will the water do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bottle has a hole near the bottom and the cap is on tight. Will the water run out? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen with the cap on, and why?
good: It will run out because it is heavy.
It will stop because the cap is shut.
It will dribble and then stop.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people say it will run out. A guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guess at the top of the table. One child: do all the jobs with your grown-up. Two to four children: share one bottle in turns as holder (finger on the hole), timer and recorder, and swap after each test. With four children, make a second bottle with the same hole and compare the two.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle with a Hole. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up lays the bottle on a folded towel and twists the needle through the side, about 4 centimetres from the bottom. Make the hole as thin as the needle, about 1 millimetre. Twist the needle once round to open the hole a little. Dry the bottle.
flow.say: I will make the hole. I push the point in with a twist, and I keep my other hand well away. The hole should be only as thin as the needle.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a small hole near the bottom. Keep your hands away.
flow.parent: A hole about 1 to 1.5 millimetres wide is best, which is what a sewing needle gives. A matchstick-wide hole (2 millimetres or more) is too big: the water keeps glugging out, with air bubbles going in through the same hole, even with the cap on. If that happens, put a piece of tape over half of the hole. A hole that is too small makes the flow with the cap off thin and slow, so be patient. Plastic can spring back and close a hole, so twist the needle.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the hole near the bottom of the bottle.

flow.do: Hold the bottle over the basin. Cover the hole with tape or a finger. Fill the bottle with water to three quarters full. Screw the cap on very tight. Lift your finger and count the seconds. Do this three times, and write down the longest and the shortest time the water ran.
flow.say: Finger on the hole. Fill the bottle three quarters full. Screw the cap on very tight. Now lift your finger. Count the seconds the water keeps coming out. Stop at thirty.
flow.kid: Finger on the hole. Cap on tight. Lift your finger. Count the seconds.

good: It came out for a moment and then stopped.
It dribbled and then stopped.
It stopped by itself.

flow.parent: You will usually see a few drops, or a short squirt lasting one or two seconds, and then nothing. If the water keeps running, the cap is not tight or the hole is too wide. Screw the cap harder first. A very thin bottle may squash a little and let a bit more out. That is fine, so write down what you see. If the water glugs out, the hole is too wide.

check.q: The water stopped running with the cap on. What changed inside the bottle?
options: The air at the top had more room, so it pushed less on the water
The cap pushed the water back
check.why: A little water leaving gave the air at the top more room, so it spread out and pushed less. The air outside pushed in at the hole as hard as the water pushed out. If you picked the cap pushing, check what happens when the cap comes off.

flow.context: In this step, you test the bottle with the cap on tight and count how long the water runs.

flow.do: Hold the bottle over the basin again, with the hole covered by a finger. Take the cap off. Lift your finger and count the seconds. After ten seconds, screw the cap back on while the water is still running.
flow.say: Same bottle. This time the cap is off. Lift your finger and count. After ten seconds, quickly screw the cap back on. What happens to the water?
flow.kid: Cap off. Lift your finger. Count. After ten seconds, screw the cap on.

ask.q: What did the water do with the cap off, and then when you put the cap back on?
good: It kept running with the cap off.
It stopped when the cap went back on.
The cap made it stop.

flow.parent: With the cap off, the water should keep running until the level drops to the hole. With a thin hole this takes several minutes, so do not wait for it: stop counting at 30. With the cap screwed back on, the flow should stop in a second or two.
flow.context: In this step, you take the cap off and see the water run, then put the cap back on and see it stop.

flow.do: Cover the hole with tape or a finger and top up the bottle to three quarters full. Screw the cap on tight. Take your finger off the hole. Gently squeeze the sides of the bottle, then let go.
flow.say: Fill it up again, cap on tight. Hold your finger on the hole. Lift it, then squeeze the sides gently. What does the water do? Now let go. Look at the hole.
flow.kid: Cap on tight. Lift your finger. Squeeze the bottle. Let go. Watch the hole.

ask.q: What did you see at the hole when you let go of the squeezed bottle?
good: Bubbles of air went in.
The water stopped squirting and a bubble went in.
Air went into the bottle.

flow.parent: When you squeeze, the water squirts out. When you let go, the bottle springs back, and a bubble of air is pushed in through the hole. It is the air outside pushing in.
flow.context: In this step, you squeeze the bottle and let go, and look for a bubble of air at the hole.

flow.do: A grown-up makes a second hole high on the bottle, 2 centimetres above the water line. Cap on tight. Lift your finger from the bottom hole and count the seconds.
flow.say: Now a second hole, high up, above the water. Cap on tight, and finger off the bottom hole. Will the water stop this time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a second hole, high up. Put the cap on and take your finger off the bottom hole. Count. What happens?

ask.q: The cap is on tight, but the water keeps running. Why?
good: Air comes in through the top hole.
The top hole lets air in.
The air on top is pushing again.

flow.parent: With the second hole open, the water should run steadily, as it did with the cap off. Air comes in through the top hole and pushes on the water at the top. The second hole must be above the water line. If it is below the water, water will leak out of it.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes a second hole high up, and you find out what it does with the cap on.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Fill in the table together. Then empty the bottle and dry everything.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? What did the air have to do with it?
flow.kid: Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why. Fill in your table.

ask.q: What does the bottle with a second hole high up show about air?
good: Air is pushing on the water.
Air needs to get in at the top for the water to run.
Air pushes on the water, and the water pushes back.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that the air pushed on the water at the hole, and that the water stopped when the air on top pushed less. After they have told you what they saw, explain: water running out gave the air at the top more room, so it pushed less. Soon the air outside, pushing in at the hole, was as strong as the push of the water and the air inside. Air at the top of the water is needed for water to keep running. A grown-up can show that a tin of juice with one hole runs in jerks, and with two holes runs smoothly.
flow.think: When the cap was on, what was missing at the top of the water?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you thought, what you saw and why it happened. Then you explain why the water stopped.

experiments.title: The Bottle That Squashes Itself
experiments.question: A bottle full of hot air and steam is closed and then cooled. Does it change shape? What if the cap is left off, or the bottle was never warmed?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After cooling, what will each of the three bottles look like? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Three bottles of the same kind are used. Bottle A gets hot water, a cap and then cold water. Bottle B has no hot water, but gets a cap and cold water. This is a control for the cold water. Bottle C gets hot water and cold water but no cap. This is a control for the closed cap. Everything else is the same. The only difference is whether the air inside was made warmer and then closed in.
results_table: Did it squash? (not at all, a little, a lot)
Seconds until it began to squash

materials.item: 3 thin 500 millilitre plastic water bottles with caps, all the same kind
hot water from a kettle that stopped boiling about 2 minutes ago, about 200 millilitres
a big bowl, a mug, and cold tap water with ice cubes or fridge-cold water (in hot weather the tap water can be nearly warm, and then the bottle squashes slowly)
a phone or clock with a second hand
oven gloves or a thick cloth
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and handles the hot bottles with a thick cloth. The water must not boil in the bottle. Do not use glass bottles. Keep small children back from the kettle and the steam. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three bottles at the end. Draw small arrows to show which air pushes harder on the walls of bottle A, inside or outside.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you try to make a bottle crush itself without touching it. You use hot water, a cap and cold water, and two bottles as controls.

setup.art: Three identical bottles on a table labelled A, B and C, with a jug of hot water and a bowl of cold water.
setup.caption: 1. Line up three bottles: A, B and C.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring a little hot water into bottle A and swirling it, with steam coming out.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up swirls hot water in bottle A and bottle C, then pours it out.

setup.art: Bottle A with its cap screwed on tight, and bottle C beside it with no cap.
setup.caption: 3. Cap bottle A at once, tight. Leave bottle C open.

setup.art: The three bottles standing in a bowl while a mug pours cold water over them, with bottle A crumpled and the other two smooth.
setup.caption: 4. Pour a mug of cold water over each bottle, and watch.

flow.do: Show your child the three bottles and say which is A, B and C. Explain what you will do to each one. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will do something different to each bottle. A gets hot water, a cap and cold water. B gets only a cap and cold water. C gets hot water and cold water, but no cap. What will each bottle look like at the end? Why?
flow.kid: There are three bottles. A gets hot water, a cap and cold water. B gets a cap and cold water. C gets hot water and cold water, but no cap. What happens to each? Why?

ask.q: Which bottle do you think will change, and why?
good: A, because the hot air turns to something else.
A, because it was hot and closed.
All of them, because the cold will crush them.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guesses at the top of the table. One child: do all three bottles with your grown-up. Two to four children: each child looks after one bottle (A, B or C) and one is the recorder. A grown-up does all the hot water.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle That Squashes Itself. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up pours about 100 millilitres of hot water into bottle A. Swirl it for 20 seconds, then pour it out. Right away, screw the cap on very tight. Do the same with bottle C, but leave its cap off.
flow.say: I will pour a little hot water into A and swirl it. Then I pour it out and put the cap on fast. I do the same with C but leave it open. Keep your hands away from the hot bottle.
flow.kid: A grown-up warms bottles A and C with hot water. Keep your hands away.
flow.parent: Move quickly between pouring out and capping. The steam fills the bottle and pushes some air out. If the bottle goes soft or shrinks while you swirl, the water was too hot. Use water that has cooled for a few more minutes.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up warms bottles A and C, and closes bottle A.

flow.do: Put the cap on bottle B too, without any hot water. Stand the three bottles in the empty bowl. Pour one mug of cold water over each bottle, and then more mugs, the same number on each. Aim at the sides, not into the mouth of C. Start the clock.
flow.say: Cap on B. Stand all three bottles in the bowl. Pour the same amount of cold water over each. Start the clock. Watch each bottle. Which one changes first?
flow.kid: Cap on B. Pour cold water over all three. Watch. Which changes?

ask.q: What do you see happening to bottle A?
good: It is squashing.
It is crumpling by itself.
It is making a crackling noise.

flow.parent: Bottle A should usually begin to crumple within about 5 to 60 seconds, often with a crackling noise. Pour the cold water over the top and shoulders of the bottle. If nothing happens after a minute, use colder water or ice, a thinner bottle or more hot water, and check that the cap is tight. Warm tap water in summer is the usual reason for a slow result.
flow.context: In this step, you put the three bottles in cold water and watch what happens.

flow.do: Watch for 2 minutes. Write down what happens to each bottle in the table. Then ask your child which air is pushing harder on bottle A, and why.
flow.say: Look at all three bottles. Which squashed, and which did not? Which air is pushing harder on the walls of bottle A, the air inside or the air outside? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Look at each bottle. Which one squashed? Which air pushes harder?

check.q: Bottle A squashed, but bottle C did not. What is the main difference between them?
options: Bottle A was closed, so the air inside could not be replaced as it cooled
Bottle A was a different bottle
check.why: Bottle C was open, so air came in as the air inside cooled, and the pushes stayed equal. Bottle A was shut, so the air inside pushed less and the outside air won. If you picked colder or a different bottle, check what happened to C.

flow.context: In this step, you read the results and say which air pushes harder.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then pour the cold water away. Open bottle A's cap and listen. Dry everything.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Now open the cap on bottle A and listen. What do you hear?
flow.kid: Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why. Open the cap and listen.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the air inside got cooler and pushed less on the walls, while the air outside kept pushing at the same strength, so it won. After they have said what they saw, add: the steam filled the bottle at first and pushed out some air. When it cooled, it turned back into drops of water. Cool air also pushes less. Opening the cap lets air rush in with a hiss, and the pushes match again. The bottle often stays crumpled, because the plastic has been bent. If bottle A did not squash, write that down. It is still a result, and you can try again with a thinner bottle.
flow.think: Bottle A did not get any lighter or heavier. What changed?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you thought, what you saw and why it happened. Then you explain why bottle A squashed.

activities.title: The Card on the Glass: what holds it up?

materials.item: a smooth glass or a clear plastic tumbler with a flat, wet rim
a smooth, flat card, such as a postcard, a playing card or a piece of a plastic folder, bigger than the glass opening
a big basin or a sink
a jug of water

activities.safety: Do this over a basin or a sink, because the water may fall.
activities.record: Draw the glass with the card. Draw an arrow for what pushes the card up and another for what pushes it down. Make the arrow longer for the bigger push.
activities.context: In this activity, you fill a glass, cover it with a card, and turn it upside down. You find out whether the water falls.

setup.art: A tumbler filled to the brim with water on a table over a basin, with a flat card ready beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the glass to the very top.

setup.art: A card slid over the top of the glass, with one hand pressing it flat and the other holding the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Slide the card over the top. Press it flat.

setup.art: The glass upside down over the basin with a hand lifting away from the card, and the card staying in place.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the glass upside down. Take your hand away.

setup.art: The same glass tilted sideways over the basin with the card still holding the water in.
setup.caption: 4. Tilt the glass sideways. Does the card still hold?

flow.do: Show your child the glass, the card and the basin. Ask for a guess and a reason before you start.
flow.say: I will fill this glass, put the card on top, and turn it upside down. What will happen when I take my hand away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A full glass has a card on top and is turned upside down. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the card, and why?
good: It will fall off with the water.
The water will push it off.
It will stay on.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people think the card and the water will fall. One child: do it with your grown-up. Two to four children: give each child a glass and a card, and take turns being the one who turns the glass while the others watch and the recorder draws.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Card on the Glass. You guess before you try.

flow.do: Over the basin, fill the glass to the very top. Slide the card across the rim, with no air left under it. Press the card flat. Hold the glass and card together and turn them over. Take your hand away.
flow.say: Fill the glass until it almost spills. Slide the card over the top, so no air bubble is left. Hold the card and turn the glass over. Now take your hand away slowly. What happens?
flow.kid: Fill the glass to the top. Slide the card on. Turn it over. Take your hand away.

ask.q: What happened to the card and the water? What do you think is holding the card?
good: The card stayed on and the water stayed in.
Something is pushing it up.
The air is holding it.

flow.parent: If the card falls, there was an air bubble or the card was not flat. Refill to the very top and try again. A paper card gets soggy after a minute, so be quick. A plastic card lasts longer.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the full glass upside down with the card on it, and take your hand away.

flow.do: Slowly tilt the glass over the basin until it is on its side. Look at the card. Then ask your child what they think is holding it.
flow.say: Now tilt the glass slowly onto its side. Is the card still holding? What does that tell us about the push that holds it? Does it push only up?
flow.kid: Tilt the glass. Does the card still hold? What does that tell you?
flow.parent: Do not explain the push yet. Ask them what they think. You will come back to this in the Bottle with a Hole. After that experiment, ask them to explain the card on the glass again.

check.q: The card still held when the glass was on its side. What does this show?
options: Air pushes on the card from every direction, not only up
check.why: The air pushes in every direction, so it can push sideways just as hard as upwards. If you picked 'only upwards', think about the glass on its side. If you picked 'sticky', try the trick with a card that is greasy.

flow.think: The glass is on its side and the card still holds. In which direction is the air pushing on the card?
flow.context: In this step, you tilt the glass and see whether the card still holds.

flow.do: Now leave a small air bubble under the card. Fill the glass nearly to the top, so the bubble is about the size of a pea. Turn it over the basin. Then try a bubble the size of a marble. Write whether the card held each time.
flow.say: Fill the glass but leave a small gap of air. Guess first: will the card still hold? Turn it over the basin. Now try a bigger gap. What changes?
flow.kid: Leave a small air gap in the glass. Guess whether the card will hold. Turn the glass over. Then try a bigger gap.
flow.parent: Results vary, so write down what you see. A tiny bubble sometimes still holds for a short while, and a big bubble usually makes the card fall. The air inside pushes down on the card too, so the push from below no longer wins by much.
flow.think: What does the air bubble inside do to the push on the card?
flow.context: In this step, you leave an air bubble in the glass and see whether the card holds.

activities.title: The Straw with a Hole: why it will not work

materials.item: 3 plastic straws of the same kind (not steel, and not paper)
a glass of water or juice
a sewing needle (a grown-up uses this)
a marker pen

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes, with the straw laid on a folded towel and the needle pushed away from fingers. Do not share straws. Use a clean straw for each person.
activities.record: Write the name of each straw and whether you could drink. Draw a straw in a glass, and draw arrows for the air pushing on the drink in the glass and on the drink inside the straw.
activities.context: In this activity, you try to drink through a plain straw, and then through a straw with a hole in it. You find out what the hole changes.

setup.art: Three straws laid on a table, one plain, one with a pin hole near the top and one with a pin hole near the bottom, each labelled.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a hole near the top of one straw and near the bottom of another.

setup.art: A child sipping from a glass of juice through a plain straw, the juice rising in the straw.
setup.caption: 2. Sip through the plain straw. Does the juice come?

setup.art: A child sipping through the straw with the hole near the top, the juice not rising, and a finger about to cover the hole.
setup.caption: 3. Sip through the straw with the top hole. What happens?

setup.art: The same straw with a finger covering the hole and juice rising in the straw.
setup.caption: 4. Cover the hole with a finger. Sip again.

flow.do: Show your child the three straws. Say that you will make a hole in two of them. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: One straw has no hole. One will have a hole near the top, and one near the bottom. Which straws can you drink through? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are three straws. Two have a hole. Which can you drink through? Why?

ask.q: Which straws will work, and why?
good: The plain one, because it has no hole.
All of them, because the straws are still straws.
None of the straws with a hole.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. One child: do it with your grown-up. Two to four children: each child gets their own three straws marked with their name, and one glass of water or juice is shared by pouring a little into a cup for each.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Straw with a Hole. You guess before you try.

flow.do: A grown-up makes a hole as wide as a matchstick near the top of one straw. Then the grown-up makes another hole, 2 centimetres from the bottom of a second straw. Mark them T for top and B for bottom.
flow.say: I will make a hole near the top of this straw, and one near the bottom of that one. I mark them T and B. Keep your hands clear.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the holes. Mark the straws T and B.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the holes in two straws.
flow.parent: A hole about as wide as a matchstick is easy to make with a sewing needle if you twist it. Mark T and B with a pen.

flow.do: Sip from the glass with the plain straw. Then try straw T, and then straw B. Write down which straws you could drink through. Then cover the hole in straw T with a finger and sip again. Last, lift straw B slowly up the glass until the hole comes above the juice, and sip as you lift.
flow.say: Sip with the plain straw first. Now straw T. Now straw B. Which ones worked? Last, put a finger over the hole in T and sip again. What changes?
flow.kid: Sip with each straw. Which work? Cover the hole in T. Sip again.

ask.q: What happened with straw T, and what happened when you covered the hole?
good: Nothing came up, and then it worked.
It stopped working with the hole open.
The finger made it work.

flow.parent: Straw T should be hard or impossible to drink with, and the plain straw should work. Straw B, with the hole low down, usually works, because the hole is under the juice and no air gets in. If the juice leaks, hold the straw deeper in the glass. If straw T works a little, the hole may be too small, so make it a little wider. Straw B should stop working as soon as its hole comes out above the juice, and that shows that any hole above the juice lets air in.

check.q: Straw T did not work, but it worked with a finger over the hole. What does the hole do?
options: It lets air in, so the air in the straw pushes as hard as the air outside
check.why: The hole let air into the straw above the juice, so the push on the juice inside the straw matched the push outside. No difference means no lift. If you chose 'lets juice out', note that the hole is above the juice in straw T.

flow.context: In this step, you sip through each straw and cover the hole.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask whether the straw pulls the drink or something else lifts it.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think the hole stopped the straw? Does the straw pull the drink, or is something else lifting it?
flow.kid: Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why. Does the straw pull?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that sipping takes some air out of the straw, and the air outside pushes the juice up. A hole lets air in, so the push inside matches the push outside. After they have said what they saw, explain: the straw does not pull the juice. The air pushing on the juice in the glass is what lifts it, once the push inside the straw is smaller.
flow.think: You sipped just as hard through straw T, the straw with a hole near the top. Why did no juice come up?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you thought, what you saw and why it happened.

activities.title: The Suction Hook: how much can the air hold?

materials.item: a rubber suction hook (about Rs 30 to 80 at a hardware shop)
a smooth, clean, flat tile or a mirror at about waist height, and a rough or painted wall to compare
a bucket with a handle
a jug of water, and a 1-litre bottle to measure it
an old towel to put on the floor under the bucket
a ruler and paper

activities.safety: Fix the hook no higher than your waist, wear slippers or shoes, and stand to the side, because the bucket may fall. Do not go above 3 litres of water in the bucket. Put a towel on the floor, and do this in a bathroom or kitchen where spills do not matter.
activities.record: Write the number of litres the hook held before it fell. Measure across the cup of the hook. Draw the hook on the tile with arrows for the air pushing it flat.
activities.context: In this activity, you stick a rubber suction hook onto a tile and hang a bucket of water on it. You find out how heavy a weight the air can hold, and compare it with what the sums say.

setup.art: A rubber suction hook being pressed flat onto a smooth tile on a wall with a child's palm.
setup.caption: 1. Wet the rim. Press the hook onto the tile.

setup.art: A bucket with a little water hanging from the suction hook, with a towel on the floor below.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the empty bucket on the hook.

setup.art: A child pouring one litre of water from a bottle into the bucket on the hook.
setup.caption: 3. Add water, one litre at a time.

setup.art: The hook and the bucket on the towel on the floor, and a child writing the number of litres.
setup.caption: 4. Note the number of litres when the hook falls.

flow.do: Show your child the hook, the tile and the bucket. Ask for a guess and a reason about how many litres it can hold.
flow.say: This rubber hook will stick to the tile. How many litres of water in this bucket do you think it can hold before it falls? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A suction hook is stuck on a tile. How many litres of water can it hold? Why?

ask.q: How many litres do you think it can hold, and why?
good: Not many, because it is only rubber.
A lot, because it sticks hard.
It depends on how well it is pressed on.

flow.parent: One litre of water has a mass of 1 kilogram. Write the guess in litres. Do not correct it. One child: do it with your grown-up. Two to four children: one pours, one watches the hook, one writes the numbers, and swap after each round.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Suction Hook test. You guess before you hang the bucket.

flow.do: Wet the rim of the hook and press it flat on the tile for 5 seconds. Pull gently on the hook with your fingers to test it. Hang the empty bucket.
flow.say: Wet the rim, press the hook flat and count to five. Pull it gently. Does it hold? Now hang the empty bucket on it.
flow.kid: Wet the hook. Press it flat. Hang the empty bucket.
flow.parent: If the hook slides off, the tile may be rough or dusty. Wipe the tile, wet the rim again and use a smoother place, such as a mirror or a glass door.
flow.context: In this step, you stick the hook on and hang the empty bucket.

flow.do: Pour in one litre of water. Wait 10 seconds. Pour in another litre. Keep going up to 3 litres, or until the hook falls. Write the number of litres each time. Then press the hook onto a rough or painted wall. Guess how many litres it will hold there, and pour again. Compare the tile and the wall.
flow.say: Pour in one litre. Wait ten seconds. Is it still holding? Pour in another. Keep going, and write down how many litres it holds. Stop at three litres.
flow.kid: Add one litre. Wait. Is it holding? Add another. Stop at three.

ask.q: What do you think is holding the hook up?
good: The air is pushing it onto the tile.
The rubber is sticky.
There is no air under the cup.

flow.parent: Cheap hooks typically hold about 0.5 to 2 kilograms for a short time, and some hold more. The bucket itself adds a little weight. The hook may slowly slide down over a minute or two. That is fine. Write the highest number of litres it held for ten seconds. On a rough wall the hook usually holds much less or not at all, because air leaks in under the rim.
flow.context: In this step, you add water to the bucket a litre at a time and see how much the hook holds.

flow.do: Measure across the hook's cup in centimetres. Ask your child to work out the area of the circle on the tile. Use half the width times half the width times three. Then work out the push of the air.
flow.say: Measure across the cup. Half of that is the radius. Multiply the radius by itself, and then by three. That is the area in square centimetres. About one kilogram of air pushes on each square centimetre. How big is the push?
flow.kid: Measure the cup. Work out its area. Air pushes with 1 kilogram on each square centimetre.
flow.parent: A cup 4 centimetres wide has a radius of 2. 2 times 2 times 3 is about 12 square centimetres. That is a possible push of about 12 kilograms. Real hooks hold much less, because some air gets under the rim and the rubber bends. The number from the sum is the most a perfect hook could hold.
flow.think: The sum gives a very big number. The hook held far less. Why?
flow.context: In this step, you work out the most that the air could hold, and compare it with what the hook held.

activities.title: Hill Station Bottle: if you go up a hill, or fly

materials.item: an empty 500 millilitre thin plastic bottle with a cap, a ruler and a piece of string
a sealed packet of chips or biscuits (keep it sealed and do not eat from it)
a trip up a hill (for example, Ooty, Munnar, Kodaikanal, Shimla or Darjeeling) or a flight. A tall lift is not enough: the change is too small to see in a bottle

activities.safety: Do this only on a trip you are making anyway. Do not go anywhere unsafe for it.
activities.record: Draw the bottle and the packet at the bottom, at the top and back at the bottom. Write how your ears felt on the way.
activities.context: This activity is for when you go up a hill or take a flight. You close a bottle at one height and see what happens at another. It is an extra activity, so do it only if you have the chance.

setup.art: A child at the bottom of a hill screwing the cap on an empty bottle next to a packet of chips.
setup.caption: 1. At the bottom, close the bottle and note how the packet looks.

setup.art: The same bottle and packet at the top of the hill, the packet puffed up and the bottle slightly swollen.
setup.caption: 2. At the top, look at the packet and the bottle.

setup.art: A child at the top of the hill unscrewing the bottle cap, with a small puff of air shown.
setup.caption: 3. Open the cap at the top, then close it again.

setup.art: The same bottle back at the bottom, squashed in the middle.
setup.caption: 4. Back at the bottom, look at the bottle.

flow.do: At the bottom of the hill, close the empty bottle tightly and look at the sealed packet of chips. Ask your child to guess what both will look like at the top, and why. Measure how thick the packet is with a ruler. Measure round the middle of the bottle with the string.
flow.say: We are going up the hill. This bottle is closed, and so is the packet. What will they look like at the top? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bottle is closed at the bottom of the hill, and the packet is sealed. What changes at the top? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the packet and the bottle at the top, and why?
good: The packet will puff up because the air is thinner.
They will stay the same.
The bottle will swell.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down before you set off. One child: do it with your grown-up. Two to four children: one looks after the bottle, one the packet, one the ruler and string.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hill Station Bottle. You close the bottle at the bottom and guess before you climb.

flow.do: At the top, look at the packet and the bottle. Feel your ears. Open the cap and listen, then close it again. Measure the packet and the string round the bottle again.
flow.say: We are at the top. Look at the packet. Look at the bottle. Did your ears pop on the way? Open the cap and listen. What happens?
flow.kid: At the top, look at the packet and the bottle. Open the cap of the bottle and listen.

ask.q: What did you see and hear at the top?
good: The packet puffed up.
The bottle was a bit swollen and let out a hiss.
My ears popped.

flow.parent: At 2,000 metres the air pushes about one fifth less than at sea level, so a sealed packet typically puffs up by a few millimetres, which you can see and measure. The bottle may swell slightly. When you open the cap at the top, you may hear air hiss out. That is the air that was shut in at the bottom.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the packet and the bottle at the top and open the cap.

flow.do: Close the bottle tightly at the top. Bring it back down, and look at the bottle. Ask your child to say why it changed.
flow.say: Now the bottle is closed again, and we go back down. What will it look like at the bottom? Why? Tell me what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Close the bottle at the top. Go back down. Look at it. Why did it change?
flow.parent: After they have said their ideas, explain: at the top the air was thin, and we shut it in. At the bottom, the air outside pushes harder than the thin air inside, so it squashes the bottle. Ears pop for the same reason: the push of the air changes faster than your ear can adjust.
flow.think: Which air is pushing harder on the bottle at the bottom, the air inside or the air outside?
flow.context: In this step, you close the bottle at the top and see what happens when you go back down.

projects.title: A Jar Barometer: watch the air's push for a week

materials.item: a clean glass jar or tumbler with a wide mouth
a balloon, cut open so it makes a flat sheet
a rubber band
a long plastic drinking straw (15 centimetres or more) and a small piece of sticky tape
a card, a ruler and a pencil
a place that stays at one temperature, out of the sun and away from the fan

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the balloon. Keep the jar away from the edge of a shelf.

schedule.what: Make the barometer. Stretch the balloon over the jar, tape on the straw, and put it in a steady place.
