Mark where the straw points. Look at the sky. Write what the weather is.
Mark the straw again and write the weather.
Mark the straw and write the weather.
Mark the straw and write the weather.
Mark the straw and write the weather.
Look at all the marks. Check them against the weather. Did the straw tip go down before rain?

projects.record: Draw a table with the day, where the straw points in centimetres on the card, and the weather. At the end, draw a line graph of the marks.
projects.context: In this project, you make a simple barometer from a jar and a balloon and watch it for a week. You see whether the push of the air changes from day to day.

setup.art: A jar with a sheet of balloon rubber stretched tight across its mouth and held with a rubber band.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch the balloon sheet tight over the jar. Hold it with a rubber band.

setup.art: A straw taped flat to the centre of the balloon sheet, with its tip sticking out past the edge of the jar.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a straw to the middle of the balloon, sticking out sideways.

setup.art: A card with a scale of centimetres standing behind the straw tip, on a shelf by a window.
setup.caption: 3. Put the card behind the straw tip, and mark where it points.

setup.art: The same barometer on another day with the straw tip higher on the card and a cloudy sky outside.
setup.caption: 4. Mark the tip every day, and write the weather.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess what the straw will do over the week and why. Show them the jar, the balloon and the straw.
flow.say: We are going to build a machine that feels the air's push. If the air pushes harder one day and less the next, what do you think the straw will do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will make a barometer from a jar, a balloon and a straw. Will the straw move over a week? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will make the straw move?
good: The air pushing on the balloon.
The weather.
The air inside the jar pushing out.

flow.parent: The jar traps a fixed amount of air. When the air outside pushes harder, the balloon is pushed in and the straw tip goes up. When the push outside is lower, the balloon bulges out and the straw tip goes down. Warmth also moves the straw, because it makes the air in the jar push more. So keep the jar out of the sun and away from the fan. One child: do it with your grown-up. Two to four children: build one jar together and take turns on the daily mark, or build two jars and compare them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Jar Barometer. You guess before you build.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the balloon open to a flat sheet. Stretch it very tight over the mouth of the jar. Fix it with the rubber band. Tape the straw flat across the middle of the sheet. It lies across the rim of the jar, and one end sticks out sideways. Let two thirds of the straw stick out past the rim. Then a small push makes a big move at the tip.
flow.say: Cut the balloon so it opens flat. Stretch it tightly over the jar and hold it with the rubber band. Tape the straw to the middle, with one end out past the edge. Make sure the jar is sealed.
flow.kid: Stretch the balloon over the jar. Tape on the straw. Seal it well.
flow.parent: Make the sheet as tight as a drum. Close the jar on a day when the weather is steady, if you can. Stand the card behind the straw tip, and use a ruler to mark a scale. Put a small piece of tape on the card to mark the first reading.
flow.context: In this step, you build the barometer from a jar, a balloon and a straw.

flow.do: Each day at the same time, mark where the straw tip points on the card. Write the weather. On the last day, compare the marks with the weather and, if you can, with the pressure number in a weather app.
flow.say: Every day, at the same time, mark the tip of the straw. Write down the weather. After a week, look at all the marks. When did the tip rise? When did it fall? What was the weather then?
flow.kid: Mark the straw every day. Write the weather. After a week, compare.
flow.parent: The movements are small, typically a few millimetres, and heat moves them too. If the tip goes up every afternoon and down every night, that is warmth, not weather. That is why we keep it in a steady place and read it at the same time. A weather app shows pressure in hectopascals (sea-level pressure), and a normal day is about 1,000 to 1,020. A fall over a day or two often goes with clouds or a storm. A single week may not show a clear pattern. Say so honestly.
flow.think: Does a falling reading go with cloud and rain where you live?
flow.context: In this step, you read the barometer every day for a week and compare it with the weather.

challenges.title: Empty the Bucket Without Lifting It
challenges.problem: A full bucket of water stands on a table. A second, empty bucket stands on the floor beside it. Move all the water into the lower bucket without lifting, tipping, scooping or pouring, and without touching the water with a cup.
constraints: You may not lift or tip either bucket.
You may not use a cup, a spoon or a pump to move the water.
You may use a clear tube or pipe about 1 metre long, and your hands.
Do not suck the water with your mouth, because it can be dirty.
materials: a bucket of water on a table or a stool
an empty bucket on the floor beside it
a clear plastic tube or an aquarium pipe about 1 metre long
general: Fill the tube with water by dipping it in the bucket, cover both ends with your thumbs, and then put one end in the high bucket and the other in the low bucket. This is a siphon.
Fill the tube with water from a tap first, then move it with both ends closed.
Make the low end lower than the water level in the high bucket.
creative: Use a strip of wet cloth or a thick rope that hangs over the rim into the lower bucket. It moves the water slowly, but it moves it.
Make a longer path with two tubes joined together so the water crosses a chair.
Find how high the bend in the tube can go before the water stops, and say why it stops.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own way to empty the bucket. Test it. Change one thing, such as how high the bend is or how long the tube is, and test it again. Which design worked fastest? What did you learn about what moves the water?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about moving water without lifting it. It uses a tube, and the push of the air.

setup.art: A full bucket on a stool, an empty bucket on the floor and a clear tube lying beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A full bucket up high, an empty one down low, and a tube.

setup.art: A child dipping the whole tube in a basin, then holding a thumb over each end.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the tube with water. Cover both ends with your thumbs.

setup.art: The tube with one end in the high bucket and the other end in the low bucket, and water flowing through.
setup.caption: 3. One end in each bucket. Lift your thumbs. Watch.

flow.do: Show your child the buckets and the tube. Read out the problem. Ask for a plan and a reason before they try anything.
flow.say: We have to empty the top bucket into the bottom one without lifting or pouring it. Here is a tube. How could we do it? Why do you think that will work?
flow.kid: Empty the top bucket with no lifting. You have a tube. What is your plan?

ask.q: What is your plan, and why do you think it will work?
good: Put one end in each bucket.
Fill the tube first.
Make the low end lower than the water.

flow.parent: Let them try their own ideas. Do not give the siphon away yet. Let them find that an empty tube does nothing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge. You make a plan before you try.

flow.do: Let your child try their plan. If they get stuck, suggest they fill the tube with water before they use it. Test each idea and note what happens.
flow.say: Try your plan. If it does not work, ask why. What would happen if the tube were already full of water? Where must the low end of the tube be?
flow.kid: Try your plan. If it fails, fill the tube first. Keep the top end under water. Let the low end hang lower, in the empty bucket.
flow.parent: The tube must be full of water, with no air bubbles, and the outlet end must be lower than the water level in the top bucket. If the water stops, an air bubble has probably got in. Fill the tube again and try once more.
flow.context: In this step, you test your plan and fix what goes wrong.

flow.do: When the water flows, lift the outlet end higher than the water in the top bucket and see what happens. Then lower it again. Ask your child why the water behaves this way.
flow.say: Now lift the low end higher than the water in the top bucket. What happens? Lower it again. What happens? Why do you think it matters which end is lower?
flow.kid: Lift the low end up. Lower it again. What happens each time?
flow.parent: When the outlet is lower than the water surface in the top bucket, the water flows. When it is higher, the flow stops or runs backwards. Scientists still argue about the exact reason a siphon works, so tell your child that this is a good question and that nobody has the full answer yet.
flow.think: Does something pull the water, or is something pushing it?
flow.context: In this step, you change the height of the outlet and see how the water responds.

items.p: Air is pushing on this page right now. In which directions does it push?
items.why: Air particles fly in every direction, so the push is the same in every direction. 'Only down' is a common idea, because we think of the weight of the air above. In the Card on the Glass, the card held even when the glass was on its side.
opts: Only down, because of its weight
In every direction, up, down and sideways
Only up

items.p: We do not notice the air pushing on us because the push is too small to matter.
items.why: False. The push is big, about 1 kilogram on every square centimetre. We do not notice it because it is balanced by the push of the air and water inside our bodies.

items.p: At sea level, air pushes with about ____ kilogram of weight on each square centimetre.
items.why: The air above one square centimetre weighs about 1 kilogram, and it pushes with that weight. On a hand of 70 square centimetres, that is about 70 kilograms.

items.p: A full glass has a card on it and is turned upside down. The card stays on. What is the best reason?
items.why: The push of the air is about 100 times bigger than the weight of the water in a tumbler. If you chose glue, think of the tilted glass, where the card still held. If you chose heavier, a light card works too.
opts: The air below pushes up on the card much harder than the water pushes down
The water sticks the card on like glue
The card is heavier than the water

items.p: Match each thing to what really makes it happen.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In each case, air pushes from the side with more air. Nothing pulls from an empty place.
pairs: A drink rising in a straw
Air pushing on the drink in the glass
A suction hook staying on a tile
Air pushing the cup flat against the tile
Air pushing the water into the dropper
Outside air pushing harder than the cooler air inside

items.p: Does the air push more or less in each place than at a beach in Chennai? Sort the places.
items.a: as given
items.why: Higher places have less air above them, so the air pushes less. Places below sea level have more air above them, so it pushes a little more.
items: The shore of the Dead Sea, which is below sea level
The peak of Doddabetta near Ooty
A valley floor close to the sea
A high mountain pass in the Himalayas
A mine shaft 500 metres below the ground

items.p: A capped bottle has a small hole low down. The water runs and then stops. Put what happens in the right order.
a: Water starts to run out of the hole
The air at the top has more room and pushes less
The air outside pushes in at the hole as hard as the water pushes out
items.why: A little water leaves, and the air at the top spreads out and pushes less. When the push outside matches the push of the water and the thinner air inside, the water stops.

items.p: A postcard is 15 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide. What is its area, in square centimetres?
items.why: 15 times 10 is 150. The area is 150 square centimetres. With about 1 kilogram of air on each square centimetre, that is about 150 kilograms of push on one side.

items.p: In your own words, explain why you do not notice the air pushing on your hand, even though the push is about 70 kilograms.
items.a: The air pushes on one side of my hand, and the air and body fluids push back on the other side with the same strength. The pushes are balanced, so my hand does not move and I do not notice it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pushes are balanced: the push from outside and the push from inside cancel. A weaker answer says the push is small, which is not true.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A drink rising in a straw, a suction hook on a tile, a dropper filling, a cycle tyre being pumped up.
items.a: The cycle tyre being pumped up, because the air inside pushes harder. In the other three, the outside air pushes harder.
items.why: In the straw, the hook and the dropper, the air inside is thinner and the outside air wins. In the pumped tyre, more air has been squeezed in, and the air inside pushes out harder than the air outside.

items.p: When you sip through a straw, the straw pulls the drink up.
items.why: False. Sipping takes air out of the straw, so less air pushes on the drink inside. The air pushing on the drink in the glass lifts it. A hole in the straw shows this, because you sip just as hard but the drink does not rise.

items.p: In the Straw with a Hole, one straw had a hole near the top and another had no hole. What is the plain straw there for?
items.why: A control changes nothing, so it shows what happens normally. Then you can say that any difference in the other straw came from the hole.
opts: It is the control, to show what happens with no hole
It is the straw that will break
It is the straw to drink from first

items.p: Someone says: 'The card stayed on the glass because the card was wet.' How could you test whether this is right? Say what you would change and what you would keep the same.
items.a: Try the card dry and wet on the same full glass. Keep the glass, the water and the card the same, and change only whether the card is wet.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, wet or dry, and keeps the glass, the water and the card the same. Then, any difference comes from the wet card.

items.p: Draw a full glass upside down with a card under it. Draw one arrow for the push of the air and one for the push of the water. Make the arrow longer for the bigger push.
items.a: A glass upside down with a card. A long arrow pointing up on the card for the air. A very short arrow pointing down for the water.
items.why: The air pushes up with about 100 times more force than the water pushes down. A strong drawing shows a very long arrow up and a very short arrow down.

items.p: Two children each sipped juice through a straw. They are arguing about how the juice rises.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and describes a test, such as a straw with a hole that is covered and uncovered.
items.why: The second view fits the evidence. A hole in the straw stops the juice, though the sip is just as strong. If the straw pulled the juice, as the first view says, the pull would be the same with or without a hole.

views.says: The straw pulls the juice up, because I can feel my mouth pulling.
The air pushes the juice up. My mouth only takes the air out of the straw.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What test could you do to find out?

items.p: A sealed packet of chips swells as the car climbs to Munnar. What is the best reason?
items.why: Higher up, there is less air above, so the push outside falls. The air shut inside still pushes as before, so the packet swells. If you picked gas from the chips, remember that a sealed empty bottle also swells, and it has no chips in it.
opts: The air outside pushes less up there, so the air inside pushes the packet out
The chips make more gas as it gets cooler
The packet gets heavier

items.p: Torricelli's tube was filled with mercury and not with water. What is the main reason?
items.why: Water would need a tube more than 10 metres tall. Mercury is much heavier, so a short column of it balances the same push.
opts: Mercury is about 13.6 times heavier than water, so the tube needs to be only about 76 centimetres tall
Mercury does not evaporate
Mercury is shiny and easy to see

items.p: The air can hold up a column of water 10.3 metres tall, which is 1,030 centimetres. Mercury is 13.6 times heavier than water. About how tall, in centimetres, is the mercury column? Round to the nearest whole number.
items.why: 1,030 divided by 13.6 is about 76. The heavier liquid makes a column 13.6 times shorter.

items.p: At the top of Mount Everest, the air pushes about ____ of what it pushes at sea level.
items.why: The air is very thin at the top of Everest. The push is about one third of the push at sea level.

items.p: A stronger pump on top of a well can lift water from 15 metres down.
items.why: False. The push of the air can lift water only about 10 metres, and real pumps manage 7 or 8. A stronger pump at the top makes no difference. The pump has to be put down in the water.

items.p: A door is 200 centimetres tall and 100 centimetres wide. About how many kilograms of air push on one side of it?
items.why: 200 times 100 is 20,000 square centimetres. With about 1 kilogram on each, that is about 20,000 kilograms, which is 20 tonnes. The other side pushes with the same, so the door does not move.

items.p: A vacuum cleaner is switched on and dust goes in. Which sentence is best?
items.why: The machine lowers the push inside the pipe. The air in the room pushes the dust and air along the pipe. An empty space has nothing to pull with.
opts: The machine lowers the push inside, and the air in the room pushes the dust in
The machine pulls the dust with an invisible rope
The empty space inside the machine pulls the dust

items.p: A sealed packet of chips is taken by car from Chennai to Ooty. Put what happens in the right order.
a: The packet is sealed at sea level
The car climbs, and the air outside gets thinner
The air outside pushes less on the packet
The air inside pushes harder than outside, and the packet puffs up
items.why: The air inside the packet stays the same, but the push outside falls as the car climbs. Then the inside wins and the packet swells.

items.p: For each thing, which pushes harder: the air outside, or the air or gas inside? Sort them.
items.a: as given
items.why: In the crushed bottle, the straw and the hook, the air inside is thinner, so the outside air wins. In the others, more air is squeezed inside, so the inside air wins.
items: A puffed-up chips packet on a hill
A suction hook held on a tile
A closed bottle of fizzy drink
A drink rising in a straw

items.p: A friend says that a straw with a hole stops working because the hole makes the straw weaker. Describe a test that would check this idea. Say what you would change and what you would keep the same.
items.a: Make two holes of the same size, one above the juice and one below the juice, in two straws of the same kind. Try both in the same glass. If weakness were the cause, both would fail. Only the hole above the juice lets air in.
items.why: A good test keeps the straw, the glass and the hole size the same, and changes only where the hole is. The hole under the juice does not let air in, so the straw still works. That shows that the hole is not making it weak. It is letting air in.

items.p: Draw a straw standing in a glass of juice. Draw an arrow for the air pushing on the juice in the glass and another for the air pushing on the juice inside the straw while you sip. Which arrow is longer?
items.a: A straw in a glass. A long arrow pointing down on the juice in the glass. A shorter arrow pointing down on the juice in the straw. The arrow in the glass is longer.
items.why: While you sip, the air in the straw is thinner, so it pushes less. The air on the juice in the glass pushes harder, so its arrow is longer, and it lifts the juice.

items.p: Going down 10 metres in a lake adds as much push as all the air above us. Why do your ears feel it in the water, when you feel nothing in the air?
items.why: Underwater, the push grows quickly as you go down, and your ears feel it before they can balance it. In the air, the push changes slowly, and the push inside your body balances it.
opts: In the air the push is balanced and changes slowly. In water the push grows fast as you go down
Water is magic
Ears only work under water

items.p: A hand has an area of 70 square centimetres. On a high hill, the air pushes with 0.8 kilogram on each square centimetre. How many kilograms of push are on one side of the hand?
items.why: 70 times 0.8 is 56. The push on the hand is about 56 kilograms, less than at sea level, where it is 70.

items.p: Two children are looking at a tall tree, 40 metres high, and wondering how water gets to the top leaves.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer notes that the air can lift water only about 10 metres, so air alone cannot lift water to 40 metres.
items.why: The second view is stronger. The push of the air lifts water only about 10 metres, so something else must lift water in a tall tree. Scientists think the leaves pull the water up, with the water held together like a chain.

views.says: The tree lifts water the way a straw does. The air pushes it all the way up.
The air can only push water about 10 metres. This tree is 40 metres tall, so something else must lift the water.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you want to find out next?

items.p: A hand pump works when the water is 6 metres down, but not when it falls to 12 metres. What is the best reason?
items.why: The air can hold up a column of water only about 10 metres tall. A pump on top cannot lift water from deeper than that.
opts: The push of the air can lift water only about 10 metres at most
The pump gets tired
Deep water is heavier

items.p: A suction cup would still stay on a tile inside a room with all the air taken out.
items.why: False. A suction cup stays on because the air outside pushes it flat. With all the air gone, nothing would push it, and it would fall off.

items.p: A tin of juice with one small hole in the top pours slowly and in jerks. With two holes it pours smoothly. Explain why, using the air.
items.a: With one hole, air has to go in through the same hole the juice comes out of, so the juice and the air take turns. With two holes, air goes in through one and juice comes out of the other, and the pushes stay balanced.
items.why: A strong answer says that air must get in as juice goes out. Otherwise the air above the juice pushes less and less, and the juice slows down or stops.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the words we use to talk about the push of air. Pressure is the push on each square centimetre. A barometer measures it. Air pressure is lower at a high altitude, and in a vacuum there is almost none.
pairs: The push on each square centimetre of a surface
A space with no air in it, or almost none
How high a place is above the sea
An instrument for measuring air pressure

worksheets.title: Worksheet 3: Reasoning with the push of air

items.p: A fish in the deep sea lives with a push on her body that is about a hundred times bigger than the push we feel. Explain why she is not crushed. What would happen to her if she were pulled to the surface very fast?
items.a: Her body is full of water and gas that push outward with the same strength as the water pushes in, so the pushes balance. Pulled up fast, the push outside gets much smaller, and the gas inside her swells and can hurt her.
items.why: A strong answer says that the push inside the fish balances the push outside, and that a quick change leaves the inside push too big. This is like the chips packet on a hill, but much bigger.

items.p: The water in a well is 9 metres down. A hand pump can lift it at sea level, but struggles at a hill station 2,000 metres up. What is the best reason?
items.why: At 2,000 metres the push of the air is about 80 percent of the push at sea level. It lifts water about 8 metres at best, and a real pump manages less. So a 9-metre lift fails.
opts: The air pushes less on the hill, so it can lift water less high
The pump is made of different metal on a hill
Water is heavier on a hill

items.p: At sea level, the push of the air can lift water about 10.3 metres. On top of Mount Everest the push is about one third as strong. About how many metres could a perfect pump lift water there? Give your answer to the nearest metre.
items.why: 10.3 divided by 3 is about 3.4, which rounds to 3 metres. At the top of Everest, a straw could lift water only about 3 metres.

items.p: Two children are arguing about the word suction.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and says that either word describes the same difference, but 'suck' can make us picture a pull that is not there.
items.why: Both have a point. Physicists say the sums come out the same whichever word you use. But the first child is right that the word suck makes us look at the gap, when the push comes from the other side.

views.says: We should say the air pushes the drink up. The word suck makes people think the empty place is pulling.
Suction is a fine word. It means the same pressure difference, and the sums come out the same.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? Does it matter which word we use?

items.p: A suction hook has a cup 6 centimetres wide. Use area = 3 times radius times radius to work out the most that the air could hold, in kilograms. Then say why a real hook holds much less.
items.a: The radius is 3. 3 times 3 times 3 is 27 square centimetres. The most the air could hold is about 27 kilograms. A real hook holds less because some air gets under the rim, and the rubber bends.
items.why: A strong answer shows the working, gets about 27 kilograms, and says why real hooks hold less: air leaks under the rim, and there is always a little air left.

items.p: Draw a bottle of water with a small hole low down and the cap on tight, after the water has just stopped running. Draw arrows for the push of the air at the hole and for the air at the top of the water.
items.a: A bottle with a hole low down. An arrow pointing in at the hole for the air outside. A smaller arrow on top of the water for the thinner air inside, with the water pushing out at the hole to balance.
items.why: The water stopped because the push in at the hole matches the push out, which is the thinner air at the top plus the weight of the water. A strong drawing shows the arrows in balance.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A pumped-up cycle tyre, a pressure cooker, a closed fizzy drink, a bottle crushed after cooling.
items.a: The crushed bottle, because the outside air pushes harder. In the other three, the push inside is bigger.
items.why: In the tyre, the cooker and the fizzy drink, more gas is squeezed into the same space, so the inside pushes harder. In the crushed bottle, the cooled air inside pushes less.

items.p: You want to know if the cap makes the water stop in the Bottle with a Hole. Which change would be a fair test?
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If the bottle or the hole also changed, you would not know whether the cap or the hole made the difference.
opts: Use the same bottle and water, with the cap on and then off
Use a big hole with the cap on and a small hole with the cap off
Use a different bottle each time

items.p: In the same air, a bigger area gets a bigger total push of air than a smaller area.
items.why: True. The air pushes on every square centimetre, so more square centimetres means a bigger total push.

items.p: A column of mercury about ____ centimetres tall balances the push of the air at sea level.
items.why: Torricelli's tube showed that the air at sea level holds up about 76 centimetres of mercury, which is 760 millimetres.

items.p: A car roof is 150 centimetres long and 100 centimetres wide. About how many tonnes of air push down on it? One tonne is 1,000 kilograms.
items.why: 150 times 100 is 15,000 square centimetres. With about 1 kilogram on each, that is 15,000 kilograms, which is 15 tonnes. The air pushes up from below and from the inside just as much, so the roof is not crushed.

items.p: Why do your ears pop when a lift rushes up a very tall building?
items.why: Going up, the push outside falls quickly. The air in the middle of your ear is still at the old push, and a little escapes with a pop to even things out.
opts: The push outside changes faster than the air in your ear can catch up
Your ears fill with water
The lift is too noisy

items.p: Explain why water boils at a lower temperature on a hill, and why dal takes longer to cook there.
items.a: On a hill, less air pushes on the water, so the water boils at a lower temperature, about 93 degrees at 2,000 metres. Cooler boiling water cooks the dal more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer links lower air pressure to a lower boiling temperature, and a lower temperature to slower cooking. A pressure cooker does the opposite. It raises the push so the water gets hotter than 100 degrees.

items.p: Put in the right order what happens when you sip a drink through a straw.
a: You make the space inside your mouth bigger
The air in the straw spreads out and pushes less
The air pushing on the drink in the glass is stronger than the air in the straw
The drink rises up the straw
items.why: Sipping thins the air in the straw. The air on the drink in the glass then pushes harder and lifts the drink.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether the height of the water in the bottle changes how long it runs with the cap off. Say what you change, what you keep the same, and what you measure.
items.a: Change the amount of water: half full and three quarters full. Keep the same bottle and the same hole, and keep the cap off. Measure the seconds until the level reaches the hole, or how far the stream shoots.
items.why: A good plan changes one thing, the height of the water, and keeps the bottle, the hole and the cap the same. It also says what will be measured, in numbers.

items.p: A mercury barometer is carried up a tall mountain. What will the mercury column do, and why?
items.why: Higher up, there is less air above, so the push on the dish is smaller. A smaller push holds up a shorter column.
opts: It will fall, because less air presses on the dish up there
It will rise, because the mountain is cold
It will stay the same, because mercury is heavy

quiz.p: Which statement about the push of air is correct?
quiz.why: Air particles fly in every direction, so air pushes on the top, bottom and sides of everything. If you picked 'only downwards', think about the Card on the Glass, where the card held even when the glass was tilted sideways.
opts: Air pushes on a surface from every direction
Air pushes only downwards
Air pushes only on things that are moving

quiz.p: About how hard does air push at sea level?
quiz.why: The air above one square centimetre weighs about 1 kilogram. A gram would be too small to hold up a glass of water. A tonne would crush us.
opts: About 1 kilogram on each square centimetre
About 1 gram on each square centimetre
About 1 tonne on each square centimetre

quiz.p: Why do we not notice the push of air on us?
quiz.why: Two equal pushes in opposite directions cancel, so nothing moves and we feel nothing. If you chose 'too weak', remember that it is about 70 kilograms on a hand.
opts: The push is balanced by the push of the air and fluids inside our bodies
The push is too weak to matter
Our skin has no way to detect any push at all

quiz.p: A capped bottle with a small hole low down has just stopped running. Why did it stop?
quiz.why: A little water leaving gave the air at the top more room, so it pushed less. Then the air pushing in at the hole matched the push out. If you chose the cap pushing the water back, think about what the water did when the cap was taken off.
opts: The air at the top spread out and pushed less, so the air outside balanced the water
The cap pushed the water back
The hole closed up

quiz.p: Why does a card stay on a glass that is full to the brim and turned upside down?
quiz.why: The air pushes up with about 100 times the weight of the water in a tumbler, so the card stays on.
opts: The air pushes up on the card much more than the water pushes down
The water is too thick to fall
The card is magnetic

quiz.p: Why does a straw with a hole in it not work?
quiz.why: No difference in the pushes means nothing lifts the drink. Covering the hole brings the difference back.
opts: The hole lets air in, so the push inside the straw matches the push outside
The hole makes the straw heavier
The hole lets the drink out

quiz.p: What really lifts the drink up a straw?
quiz.why: Sipping takes air out of the straw, and the air outside pushes the drink up. An empty space has nothing to pull with.
opts: Air pushing on the drink in the glass
The straw pulling
The empty space in the straw

quiz.p: What happens to air pressure as you climb a tall mountain?
quiz.why: The higher you are, the less air is above you, so the push is smaller. At the top of Everest it is about a third of the push at sea level.
opts: It gets smaller, because there is less air above you
It gets bigger, because you are nearer the sky
It stays the same everywhere

quiz.p: Why can a pump at the top of a pipe not lift water from 15 metres down?
quiz.why: The push of the air can lift water only about 10 metres at sea level. Deeper wells need the pump put down in the water.
opts: The push of the air can hold up only about 10 metres of water
The pump is too small
Water is too heavy for any pump

quiz.p: A card has an area of 80 square centimetres. About how many kilograms of air push on one side of it?
quiz.why: The air pushes with about 1 kilogram on each square centimetre. 80 times 1 is 80 kilograms.

quiz.p: In the Bottle with a Hole, which is the best way to see what the cap does?
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time, so the change in the result must come from the cap.
opts: Use the same bottle and the same hole, and change only the cap
Change the cap and the size of the hole together
Use a new bottle for each test

quiz.p: A sealed bottle is carried from the top of a hill down to the beach and it squashes. Which push is bigger on the bottle at the beach?
quiz.why: The air at the beach pushes harder than the thin hill air that was shut in. The outside wins.
opts: The push of the air outside
The push of the air inside
They are the same

applications: Drinking straws, droppers and syringes, which move liquid by lowering the push on one side.
Vacuum cleaners, which lower the push inside so the air in the room pushes the dust in.
Suction hooks, suction cups on tiles and the rubber cups that lift glass sheets in a factory.
Pressure cookers, which raise the push inside so the water boils hotter and the food cooks faster.
Barometers and weather stations, which watch the air's push to predict rain and storms.
Hand pumps, such as the India Mark II, which push the water up from down in the well, so they work from deeper than the 10-metre limit.
Aeroplane cabins, kept at the push you would feel at about 2,000 metres so passengers are comfortable.
Tyres, footballs and cycle pumps, which pack more air into a space so it pushes hard.
The Ayrton fan, designed by the engineer Hertha Ayrton in 1915 to push poison gas out of trenches by moving air.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a siphon work? Is it air pressure, or the pull of one side of the water on the other?
open_questions.why_open: Everyone agrees on what a siphon does. Physics teachers and scientists still argue about the best explanation.

open_questions.q: How do deep-sea animals keep their bodies working under a push hundreds of times bigger than the push we feel?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found chemicals in deep-sea fish that seem to protect their proteins, but they do not yet know the whole story.

open_questions.q: Is any space really empty, a perfect vacuum?
open_questions.why_open: Even in the emptiest space, scientists measure tiny pushes and flickers of energy. What is really there is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How do the tallest trees lift water more than 100 metres, when air can lift it only about 10?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think leaves pull water up in a chain, but the details are still debated and tested.

open_questions.q: Can we forecast the weather perfectly if we measure the air pressure everywhere?
open_questions.why_open: The air is made of billions of billions of particles, and a tiny difference at the start can grow into a big one. Nobody knows how far ahead a forecast can ever be right.

ask_kids: When you drink from a straw today, ask yourself what really lifts the drink.
Where in our house is a push of air working, even though we cannot see it?
Why do you think the chips packet puffs up when we drive up a hill?
If we took a straw to the Moon, what would happen when we sipped?
What would happen to a pressure cooker if the whistle were blocked?
How is the air pushing on you right now? In which directions?
Does the hand pump in our area have its working part at the top, or down in the water?
Which would you trust more: a famous old idea, or a simple test you can do yourself? Why?

jokes.j: Why did the glass refuse to spill?
jokes.a: It had a card in its pocket and the air had its back.

jokes.j: What did the straw say to the juice?
jokes.a: I don't pull you. The air does it.

jokes.j: Why was the bottle so crushed?
jokes.a: It had a big squeeze from the outside.

jokes.j: Why does a hill station chips packet look so proud?
jokes.a: It puffs up at the top.

jokes.j: Why did the suction hook stay on the tile?
Why did the barometer look worried?
Why did the pump give up at twelve metres?
Why did the tyre feel so important?
What did the vacuum cleaner say to the dust?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I'm not sucking, the room is pushing you in.

maths.problem: A card is 12 centimetres long and 9 centimetres wide. What is its area? About how many kilograms of air push on one side of it?
maths.explain: 12 times 9 is 108 square centimetres. Air pushes with about 1 kilogram on each square centimetre, so the push on one side is about 108 kilograms.
maths.context: In the Card on the Glass, the air pushes up on the card over its whole area.
maths.why_maths: The air pushes on every square centimetre, so the area tells you the total push.

maths.problem: The water in a glass 12 centimetres tall pushes down on the card with about 12 grams on each square centimetre. The air pushes up with about 1,000 grams on each square centimetre. About how many times bigger is the push of the air?
maths.explain: 1,000 divided by 12 is about 83. The push of the air is about 83 times bigger than the push of the water, so the card stays on.
maths.context: In the Card on the Glass, the card stays on because the air pushes up more than the water pushes down.
maths.why_maths: A ratio shows how much bigger one push is than the other, so you can see why the card holds.

maths.problem: In the Bottle with a Hole, the water ran for 2 seconds with the cap on. With the cap off it was still running when you stopped counting at 30 seconds. At least how many times longer did it run with the cap off?
maths.explain: 30 divided by 2 is 15. It ran at least 15 times longer, and probably much more, because it was still running when you stopped.
maths.context: In the Bottle with a Hole test, you count the seconds the water flows with the cap on and with it off. The numbers here are made up.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two times says how much longer one test ran, which shows how big the effect of the cap was.

maths.problem: A village pump can lift water up to 7 metres. In the monsoon the water is 4 metres down. In summer it falls by 1 metre every 10 days. After how many days will the pump stop working?
maths.explain: The pump stops when the water falls from 4 metres down to 7 metres down, which is a fall of 3 metres. At 1 metre every 10 days, 3 metres takes 3 times 10, which is 30 days. After that, the water is too deep for a pump at the top.
maths.context: A hand pump at the top of a pipe can lift water only about 7 or 8 metres, so it stops when the water falls below that.
maths.why_maths: Counting how far the water must fall, and how long that takes, tells a village how soon it must plan for a deeper pump.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of the air pressure readings. On which day was the pressure lowest, and by how many hectopascals did it fall between Monday and Thursday?
maths.answer: Thursday was lowest. It fell by 9 hectopascals.
maths.explain: The line is lowest at Thursday, at 1,003. On Monday it was 1,012. 1,012 take away 1,003 is 9. A falling reading often goes with clouds and rain.
maths.context: In the Jar Barometer, you mark the height of the straw each day. These are made-up readings from a weather station for the same days.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows at a glance when a reading rises and falls, which helps you see a pattern with the weather.

maths.problem: A suction hook has a cup 4 centimetres wide. Its radius is 2 centimetres. Use area = 3 times radius times radius. What is the area, and what is the most that the air could hold, in kilograms?
maths.answer: The area is 12 square centimetres, and the air could hold at most about 12 kilograms.
maths.explain: 2 times 2 is 4, and 4 times 3 is 12. With about 1 kilogram of push on each square centimetre, the most is about 12 kilograms. A real hook holds less.
maths.context: In the Suction Hook test, you hang a bucket of water on a rubber hook and compare the weight it held with the sum.
maths.why_maths: The sum gives the best possible result, so you can compare it with what the hook really held.

maths.problem: At sea level, the air can hold up 76 centimetres of mercury. On a hill where the push is three quarters as strong, how many centimetres of mercury could it hold up?
maths.explain: A quarter of 76 is 19, so three quarters is 3 times 19, which is 57. A mercury barometer on that hill would stand at about 57 centimetres.
maths.context: A barometer shows the air's push as the height of a column of mercury. The push is smaller high up, so the column is shorter.
maths.why_maths: Taking a fraction of the sea-level height predicts what a barometer will read on a hill.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,300 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle taught that nature hates an empty space, so water has to follow a pump's piston to keep any gap from opening. People believed this for almost 2,000 years. Then, in the 1600s, well-makers in Italy found that their pumps would not lift water higher than about ten metres, and no one could say why. Around 1643, Evangelista Torricelli guessed that the weight of the air was holding the water up. His helper, Vincenzo Viviani, filled a glass tube about a metre long with mercury, a liquid metal 13.6 times heavier than water, and turned it over in a dish. The mercury sank to about 76 centimetres and stopped, leaving a space at the top. In 1648, Blaise Pascal's brother-in-law, Florin Périer, carried the tube up the Puy de Dôme, a mountain in France. The higher he went, the lower the mercury stood.
how_we_found_out.who: Evangelista Torricelli and Vincenzo Viviani in Italy, and Blaise Pascal and Florin Périer in France
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The wrong idea was Aristotle's: that nature hates a vacuum and so fills every gap. The pump limit of about ten metres, Torricelli's empty space at the top of the tube, and the lower mercury on the mountain showed that the weight of air does the pushing, and that it pushes less with height.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Card on the Glass: fill the glass to the very top and slide the card on with no bubble. A paper card gets soggy after a minute, so a plastic card or a laminated sheet is better. Bottle with a Hole: a hole as thin as a sewing needle, about 1 millimetre, 4 centimetres from the bottom, is best. With a hole as wide as a matchstick the water keeps dribbling even with the cap on, and a very thin bottle may squash a little and let a bit more out. The steps say what to do. Squashing Bottle: the water must be hot but not boiling, or the bottle itself shrinks. Control bottle C shows this. Bottle A should squash within about 30 seconds, but a thick bottle may only dent, and the steps say to use a thin one. Suction Hook: small hooks typically hold about 0.5 to 2 kilograms, and the calculation shows the most that a perfect cup could hold, so the numbers do not match on purpose. Jar Barometer: the movement is a few millimetres, and heat moves it too, so keep it out of the sun. The siphon challenge works best with a clear tube that is completely full of water. The videos have no address yet. Facts to verify before the unit goes live: the Galileo pump limit of about 18 braccia, the Périer date of 19 September 1648, the Hertha Ayrton fan date of 1915, the claim that a breath holds more air particles than there are grains of sand on all the beaches, the Hughes and Richert and Binder papers on siphons, the Rig Veda 10.168 wording, and the boiling temperature of about 93 degrees at 2,000 metres.

quiz: Air pushes on a thing from every side at once, not only from above.
Air particles fly in every direction, so they hit the top, the bottom and the sides.
When you drink through a straw, your mouth pulls the drink up.
You take air out of the straw, and the air pushing on the drink in the glass lifts it.
Air pushes down on things only, because the air is above us.
A card holds water in a sideways glass too. Air pushes sideways and up as hard as down.
A straw with a small hole in its side stops working.
Air comes in through the hole, so the air outside no longer pushes harder on the drink than the air in the straw.
We do not feel air pushing on us because our body pushes back just as hard.
Fluids and air inside our body push out with the same strength, so the pushes balance.
Air pressure is the same at the top of a mountain as at sea level.
Higher up there is less air above you, so the air pushes less.
A pump at the top of a pipe cannot lift water from deeper than about ten metres.
The push of air can hold up only about ten metres of water.
Tall trees lift water to their tops using the push of the air, like a straw.
Air can lift water only about ten metres, but some trees are over a hundred metres tall.
A fall in air pressure on its own tells us that rain is coming.
Pressure alone does not tell the weather. A forecast also needs temperature, wind and water in the air.
More air particles in the same space make a bigger push.
Pressure comes from particles hitting a surface, so more hits mean more push.
odd: A straw, a vacuum cleaner and a suction hook all work because air pushes. A magnet works without air.
High places have less air above them, so the push is smaller. A beach is at sea level, where the push is biggest.
The first three stay still because the pushes on them are balanced. The speeding ball has unbalanced pushes.
Pumping, heating and squeezing make more or faster particle hits and raise pressure. Cooling slows the particles and lowers it.
The first three have almost no air inside. A pumped tyre is packed with more air than outside.
